_meta.note: The 8 Jev rubric categories, one Jev `score` question each. This file is the source of truth (scripts/jev-gate is self-contained in CI). Instructions describe ONLY what to score and the level criteria — say NOTHING about confidence: confidence is the model's own axis (its certainty in the verdict), so the rubric must never instruct, calibrate, or nudge it; a low-confidence score already routes to human sign-off. Duplication was dropped 2026-09-19 — it needs cross-file context the per-file gate cannot supply, so its scores were never decidable.
_meta.scale: Every question is a Jev `score`. Levels run 0 (worst) to 4 (best). Higher always means healthier code, so the overall score is a plain mean.

code_smells.instructions: Rate this source code for Martin Fowler-style code smells that are OBSERVABLE IN THIS FILE ALONE — each file is judged independently, so do not consider smells that require seeing other files. In scope: long methods, large classes, primitive obsession, data clumps, long parameter lists, speculative generality, and boolean/flag parameters that silently switch a function's behavior (control coupling) — a pattern easy to accumulate in TypeScript because optional booleans are cheap to add. Do NOT judge cross-file smells you cannot see from a single file, such as shotgun surgery (one change rippling across many files) or feature envy (a method more interested in another class not shown here). Higher means fewer, less harmful smells.
criteria: Riddled with smells: bloated methods and classes, primitive obsession, data clumps, long parameter lists, and/or flag-parameter control coupling throughout
Frequent smells that clearly hurt readability and make change unsafe
Some smells present but localized and low impact
Mostly clean; only minor, defensible smells remain
No meaningful code smells; cohesive and well factored

security.instructions: Rate this source code for security by the dangerous patterns VISIBLE IN THIS FILE — judge what is written here, never whether some caller you cannot see supplies attacker-controlled input. Weight heavily concrete in-file hazards that are dangerous regardless of the caller: a hardcoded secret, API key, password, or a hardcoded or reused crypto key or IV; a non-CSPRNG source (e.g. Math.random) used to generate tokens, session ids, nonces, or salts; a fast general-purpose hash (e.g. MD5/SHA-1) used for passwords; a subprocess spawned with `shell: true`, or a command or argument built by interpolating variables in this file; a SQL/NoSQL query or a filesystem path built by string-concatenating variables instead of via parameters, an allowlist, or path APIs; unsafe deserialization, or `eval`/dynamic code built from a non-literal; and an auth or permission check in this file that fails OPEN (an error, missing value, or unknown case falls through to allowed). Do NOT try to guess whether an input is attacker-controlled or whether a caller is trusted — that needs call sites you cannot see; judge only the hazard visible here. Do NOT lower the score for framework-mediated safety clearly in force in this file: parameterized or ORM-built queries, inputs validated or type-narrowed here before use, an allowlist or escaping applied on the path. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: a fixture, mock/stub, type declaration, story, or test file has no security surface of its own, so score it near the top by default. Higher means fewer dangerous patterns visible in this file.
criteria: A critical in-file hazard: a hardcoded secret or crypto key/IV, a non-CSPRNG used for a token or session id, `shell: true` or a command built from interpolated variables, a query or path built by string-concatenating variables, unsafe deserialization or eval from a non-literal, or an auth check that fails open

A serious in-file weakness, even if it needs specific conditions: e.g. a fast general-purpose hash used for passwords, or an error path here that puts a stack trace, path, or secret into a returned value or a log call
A risky in-file pattern whose severity depends on context this file does not show (e.g. a value used in a path or query whose origin is not visible here)
Only defense-in-depth nits: patterns that look risky in isolation but are validated, parameterized, or use safe APIs within this file
No dangerous patterns visible: no secrets, safe crypto and query/path APIs used, validation or escaping applied here, and errors do not embed internal detail into returned values or logs

complexity_clean_code.instructions: Rate this source code for complexity and Robert C. Martin clean-code qualities: function size and single responsibility, name clarity, and complexity as a reader would actually feel it. Judge complexity qualitatively, not by literal branch counting (exact counting is a known weak spot for this model). Prefer a cognitive-complexity lens over a cyclomatic one: nested control flow that forces a reader to hold multiple contexts at once (for example a loop containing a try/catch containing a conditional) is worse than the same number of sequential, early-return guard clauses, even when both have a similar number of branches. Higher means simpler and cleaner.
criteria: Very hard to follow: deeply nested control flow that forces holding multiple contexts at once, huge functions, unclear names
Often complex or poorly named; frequent cognitive overload from nesting or mixed concerns, even where individual branch counts look modest
Moderate complexity; some nesting or nested error handling that could flatten into guard clauses, several functions or names could be simpler
Mostly simple and well named; small focused functions with shallow, mostly linear control flow
Clean and simple: small single-purpose functions, clear names, shallow linear control flow with no nested-context reading burden

comments.instructions: Rate the comment discipline of this source code. Good comments explain non-obvious why (hidden invariants, external constraints, justified lint or type suppressions, public API doc contracts). Bad comments narrate what the code already says, add banners, leave commented-out code, or preach about workarounds instead of fixing them. A lint or type suppression is only 'justified' if the comment names the specific reason it is needed (a specific external constraint or a specific known false positive) — a suppression with no reason, or a vague one such as 'needed' or 'temp fix', counts as undisciplined. Higher means better discipline.
criteria: Pervasive narration, banners, commented-out code, or unjustified lint or type suppressions
Many comments restate the code or justify workarounds rather than fixing them
Mixed: some useful comments alongside several redundant what-comments
Mostly disciplined; only a rare redundant comment
Exemplary: comments explain only non-obvious why; no narration, no dead code; every suppression names its specific reason

testability.instructions: Rate how easily this source code can be unit tested: presence of seams, dependency injection, pure versus side-effecting logic, and avoidance of hidden global state. The single sharpest signal is whether a collaborator — a service, client, repository, or other stateful dependency — is constructed inline inside the function or class under review (a bare `new X()` buried in business logic, with no way for a caller to substitute it) versus received as a parameter or constructor argument (a seam a test can use to inject a fake). Inline construction of a collaborator is a stronger testability smell than almost any other pattern, even when the rest of the function is otherwise pure. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: testability is a category error for a fixture, mock/stub, type declaration, or story file — there is no logic to unit test, so score it near the top by default unless it does something that would genuinely make it awkward to use from a test (e.g. a hidden side effect on import). For a test file itself, judge only whether its own helpers/setup are testable, not whether the test needs testing. Apply the full bar only to application/business logic.
criteria: Untestable: hidden dependencies, collaborators constructed inline with no injection seam, global state, side effects fused with logic
Hard to test; would need heavy mocking or refactoring first, including reaching inside the module to replace an inline-constructed collaborator
Testable with some effort; a few seams missing
Mostly testable; clear seams and injectable dependencies
Highly testable: pure functions, injected dependencies, clean seams — or a non-logic file (fixture/mock/type/story) with nothing that would resist being used in a test

error_handling.instructions: Rate the error handling that is FULLY SELF-CONTAINED IN THIS FILE. Each file is scored alone, so never depend on callers, callees, or other files — judge only the handling written here and the failure paths of operations this file itself performs. Look for: catch blocks that swallow the error (an empty catch, a catch that only logs and continues past a genuine failure, or one that discards the error and returns a success-shaped or default value); over-broad catches that collapse clearly distinct failures into one; promise rejections left unhandled in this file (a floating async call or promise with no await and no .catch, or a .then with no rejection handler); and the result of an operation THIS file performs that can fail — a JSON.parse, Number()/parseInt, a file read, a network or DB call, a deserialize — used directly with no guard on its failure path. Also flag an error that places internal detail — a stack trace, file path, internal identifier, or secret — into a value this file returns or into a log/response call written here (also weighted under `security`; flagging it in both is fine). Do NOT penalize a function for not validating its plain parameters: whether a parameter is external or trusted depends on callers you cannot see, so it is out of scope. Judge validation only at boundaries THIS file itself crosses (where it parses, reads I/O, deserializes, or reads env). First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: a fixture, mock/stub, type declaration, story, or test file has no failure path of its own, so score it near the top by default. Higher means the error handling written in this file is more robust.
criteria: Failures swallowed or ignored in this file: empty or silent catches, unhandled promise rejections, or the result of an in-file parse/IO/deserialize used with no failure handling; or an error path here puts a stack trace, path, or secret into a returned value or a log call
Weak: broad catch-alls and several silent failures in the handling written here
Partial: some in-file failure paths handled, but clear gaps remain (an in-file parse or IO whose failure is unguarded, a swallowed catch)
Mostly robust; only minor gaps in the handling written here

Robust: the operations this file performs that can fail are guarded, errors propagate without leaking internal detail, and no exception is swallowed — or a non-logic file (fixture/mock/type/story/test) with no failure path of its own

concurrency_and_idempotency.instructions: Rate this source code for event-loop discipline and idempotency under retries and partial failure. A background loop, periodic poll, reconcile pass, boot sweep, or fill job that iterates a collection whose size grows with the database or workload MUST chunk its synchronous work and yield the event loop between chunks (e.g. via a yield helper) — a tight synchronous loop over an unbounded or growing collection on the shared Node event loop is a critical violation, since it can freeze every other request the process serves. Commands, lifecycle steps, and processing loops must also be idempotent: they should converge to the same end state whether run once or replayed after a crash, restart, or retry, with no double-application of a side effect (e.g. double-charging, double-inserting, re-sending a notification) on a retried attempt. A retry loop or subprocess-spawn loop with no upper bound is also a smell here. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: MOST files have no background loop, no shared-state mutation, and no retryable command — pure functions, types, UI components, tests, fixtures, mocks, stories, and config have no such surface at all. Score these near the top (4) by default; do not penalize a file for lacking yield points or idempotency guards it was never meant to have. Apply the full bar only to code that actually runs a loop over a growing collection, a periodic or background job, or a retryable command or lifecycle step.
criteria: Has a background loop, poll, reconcile pass, or retry/spawn loop that is a critical risk: a tight synchronous loop over an unbounded/growing collection with no yield, or a side effect that clearly double-applies on retry
Same surface present but only partially mitigated: yields are missing on some paths, or idempotency holds for the common case but breaks under a plausible crash or retry
Has the surface and mostly handles it correctly, but a genuine gap remains (e.g. an unbounded retry with no cap, or a lifecycle step whose idempotency is unclear)
Has the surface and handles it correctly; only a minor, defensible gap remains
No background loop, retryable command, or shared-state mutation to worry about — or, where present, it chunks/yields correctly and converges to the same end state under crash, restart, or retry

ai_slop.instructions: Rate this source code for tells that it was produced by an LLM coding agent without a human editing pass — a distinct axis from the other categories, which judge whether the code is good; this one judges whether it reads like nobody looked at it twice. Weight, in roughly this order of severity: (1) hallucinated or non-existent imports, packages, or API calls that would fail at build or runtime — the single most damning tell; (2) leftover assistant chatter or meta-commentary embedded in the file itself, e.g. 'As an AI...', 'Here is the updated function', 'I've refactored this to...', apologetic hedges ('this is a simplified version', 'note that this may not be perfect'), or a first-person voice narrating the change rather than describing the code; (3) proliferation of near-identical, differently-named helpers doing the same job (e.g. formatCurrency/formatMoney/displayPrice) instead of reusing or extending one — a machine-scale variant of copy-paste; (4) needless speculative abstraction added with no second caller or driving requirement — an interface, strategy, or config knob behind a single implementation, justified only as 'for future use' or 'for flexibility'; (5) reflexive, blanket defensiveness: a try/catch wrapped around an operation that cannot throw, or the same null/array-length guard repeated verbatim many times instead of validated once at a boundary; (6) generic placeholder naming and unfinished stubs left as if forgotten — data/result/temp/foo/item1, or a TODO/FIXME describing work the surrounding code claims is already done; (7) tutorial-density comments narrating nearly every line at a rate no working human engineer would bother with, even where an individual comment might pass a why-vs-what test in isolation — this can overlap with `comments`; flag it in both when it does, the same way an error that leaks internal detail is flagged under both `security` and `error_handling`. Calibrate decisively: a single instance of the two most damning tells — a hallucinated or non-existent import/API, or leftover assistant chatter — scores 0–1 on its own; do not wait for tells to stack. Conversely, do NOT manufacture tells: plain, terse, or unremarkable code that simply carries no tell is not slop and scores 4, and most human-edited files should land at 4 — reserve the lower bands for code where a specific tell is actually present. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: a generated file, fixture, mock, type declaration, or plain data file has no authorial voice to judge, so score it near the top by default. Higher means the code reads like a deliberate human wrote and edited it, with no AI-agent tells.
criteria: One or more damning tells: a hallucinated or non-existent import/API that would fail at build or runtime, or leftover assistant chatter/apology in the file ('Here is the updated…', 'As an AI…') — either alone lands here, no stacking required
Frequent tells a careful human editing pass would have caught, appearing more than once: renamed-duplicate helpers, speculative single-implementation abstractions, or blanket defensive wrapping
One clear, localized tell: a single placeholder name (data2/temp/foo), one try/catch around code that cannot throw, one narrated stretch of comments, or one unneeded single-use abstraction
Mostly clean; only a faint, easy-to-miss tell (one slightly generic name or a single redundant guard)

Reads as deliberately human-written and edited: naming, abstraction, and defensiveness all proportionate, no tell present — or a non-authorial file (generated/fixture/mock/type/data). Do not invent tells; clean code belongs here
